input.question: What happens if you freeze a super strong container full of water?
input.ground_truth: There are different types of “ice” depending on pressure. Typical ice is ice-I; when freezing water under sufficient pressure, different types all the way to ice-XVI have been produced, some are unstable and can’t be found in nature. Most of these are more dense than water (ie the water would shrink rather than expand). It is hypothesized that under sufficient pressure (e.g. a strong enough container shrinking in size) water would freeze into a metallic form of ice.

Question: What happens if you freeze a super strong container full of water?

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a really, really strong box, and inside the box is lots and lots of water. Now, if you put that box outside when it is super, super cold—so cold that everything turns to ice—the water inside the box will start to freeze.

But here’s the thing: when water turns to ice, it gets bigger. It’s like when you fill a cup almost to the top with water and put it in the freezer—the water pops out a little when it freezes.

Now, if the box is super strong, it might not break right away. But if the ice keeps growing and growing and there’s not enough room inside the box, the ice will push really hard against the sides of the box. If the box isn’t strong enough or if the ice pushes too hard, the box might crack or even break!

So, if you freeze a super strong container full of water, the water becomes ice and tries to get bigger. If the container can’t handle the ice getting bigger, it might break. But if it’s really, really strong, it might just hold the ice inside.
